question.prompt: Melanie computes the mean \(\mu,\) the median \(M,\) and the modes of the \(365\) values that are the dates in the months of \(2019.\) Thus her data consist of \(12\) \(1\)s, \(12\) \(2\)s, \(\ldots,\) \(12\) \(28\)s, \(11\) \(29\)s, \(11\) \(30\)s, and \(7\) \(31\)s. Let \(d\) be the median of the modes. Which of the following statements is true?

solutions.title: Bound the mean using equal-length months
solutions.explanation:
The dates \(1\) through \(28\) each occur \(12\) times, more often than any other date. They are therefore precisely the modes. Their median is
\[
d=\frac{14+15}{2}=14.5.
\]

Among \(365\) ordered values, the median is the \(183\)rd value. There are
\[
15\cdot12=180
\]
values at most \(15\), and the next \(12\) values are all \(16\). Thus \(M=16\).

To bound the mean, first imagine keeping only dates \(1\) through \(28\) in every month. These equally frequent values have mean
\[
\frac{1+28}{2}=14.5.
\]
The actual data add some \(29\)s, \(30\)s, and \(31\)s, all above this mean, so \(\mu>14.5\).

Now imagine that every month has \(31\) days. The equally frequent dates \(1\) through \(31\) have mean
\[
\frac{1+31}{2}=16.
\]
The actual data result from removing some \(29\)s, \(30\)s, and \(31\)s. Removing values above the mean lowers it, so \(\mu<16\).

Consequently,
\[
\boxed{d<\mu<M},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
